379.title: Four kinds of happiness
379.hook: having wealth, using it well, owing no debt, and being blameless (AN 4.62)
379.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use this sutta to show that householders may rightly enjoy honestly earned wealth, while counting a clear conscience as the greatest happiness; Anathapindika is remembered in the tradition as the model generous lay follower.

segments.voice: Yesterday: five trades, and your line, what your money does. Did you follow one payment and see what it supports? Day three hundred seventy-nine.

Anathapindika was a wealthy merchant in the city of Savatthi. His name means feeder of the unprotected, because of how much food he gave away. By the old story, he bought a park for the Buddha's community by covering its ground in gold coins. So when the Buddha talks to him about money, he isn't lecturing someone on thrift. He's talking to a man who has more than enough. And he tells him there are four kinds of happiness that wealth can touch, and that one of them outweighs the other three put together. Today: four kinds of happiness.
screen: `FEEDER OF THE UNPROTECTED.` → `A PARK PAVED IN GOLD.` → `ONE OUTWEIGHS THE REST.`

segments.voice: The first is the happiness of having: knowing you have wealth earned, the sutta says, by hard work, by the strength of your arms and the sweat of your brow, rightly gained. Notice that this counts as a real happiness. The Buddha doesn't tell a householder that money is shameful. The second is the happiness of using it: enjoying your wealth and doing good with it, for yourself, your family, your friends, and worthy causes. Money sitting untouched is only half a pleasure. The third is the happiness of owing nothing, no debt, large or small. A credit card bill that keeps growing shows what this one is like when it's missing. And the fourth is the happiness of blamelessness: knowing that what you've done with your body, your speech and your mind carries no fault. Then comes the verse at the end. The first three, the Buddha says, aren't worth a sixteenth part of the fourth. A sixteenth part is an old Indian idiom for a tiny fraction. So the order is clear, but it isn't a choice between them. A householder can have all four. The sutta simply ranks them. You can be wealthy, generous and debt-free, and still be uneasy if you know how the money was made. And you can have very little, owe nothing, and sleep like a stone, because there's nothing in your day you need to hide.
screen: `THE HAPPINESS OF HAVING.` · `THE HAPPINESS OF USING.` · `THE HAPPINESS OF OWING NOTHING.` · `BLAMELESSNESS OUTWEIGHS THEM ALL.` · then, large: `BLAMELESS IS BEST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Go through the four slowly, one at a time, and look for any trace of each in your own life. Something you have, however small. Something you were able to use well, or share. A debt you've paid off, or never had. And something you did this week that you don't need to hide. Rest a little longer on whichever one you find. Let it be a real happiness, the way the sutta says it is. The bell holds the time.
Four kinds of happiness. Having, using, owing nothing, and blamelessness; the Buddha tells Anathapindika the last outweighs the rest.
Your line: blameless is best. Today, note one money blessing you have, and one thing you did that you'd be glad for anyone to see. Day three hundred seventy-nine.

380.title: Four parts
380.hook: to Sigala: one part to live on, two for work, one kept for hard times (DN 31)
380.howItsDone: The Sigalovada Sutta is widely taught to lay Buddhists, especially in Theravada countries, as practical guidance for family, friendship, work and money.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four kinds of happiness, and your line, blameless is best. Which of the four did you find a trace of in your own life? Day three hundred eighty.
screen: `FOUR KINDS OF HAPPINESS — BLAMELESS IS BEST.`

segments.voice: Early morning near Rajagaha. A young man named Sigala stands with his clothes and hair still wet, bowing in six directions: east, south, west, north, down, and up. His dying father told him to do this, and he does it faithfully, without knowing why. The Buddha, walking into town for alms, stops and asks what he's doing. Then, gently, he reinterprets the whole ritual. The six directions, he says, are the people in your life. What follows is a whole sutta of advice for ordinary life, and somewhere in the middle of it, there's a budget. Today: four parts.
screen: `WET HAIR, SIX BOWS.` → `HIS FATHER'S LAST WISH.` → `THE BUDDHA STOPS TO ASK.`

segments.voice: The six directions become six relationships. East is your parents. South, your teachers. West, your spouse and children. North, your friends. Below, those who work for you. Above, spiritual teachers. For each, the Buddha lists what you owe them and what they owe you. Then, in a run of verses, he turns to money. The wise person, he says, gathers wealth the way a bee gathers nectar, a little at a time, and it grows the way an anthill grows. Then the budget. Divide your wealth into four parts. Live on one part and enjoy it. Put two parts to work in your business. Keep the fourth part saved against hard times. One for living, two for work, one for the rainy day. It's ancient advice, and it would still make sense on a spreadsheet. Notice what it assumes: that a householder will have money, should enjoy some of it, should invest in their livelihood, and should plan for misfortune. Nothing here is otherworldly. The fractions don't map neatly onto a modern paycheck, and the tradition doesn't treat them as law. Some read the two parts for work as money invested, others as the costs of running a trade. But the shape is the lesson: enjoy some, build with some, protect some, and decide on purpose. The commentary on this sutta, traditionally credited to Buddhaghosa, calls it the discipline of the householder. Monks have their rules. This is a lay person's.
screen: `SIX DIRECTIONS, SIX RELATIONSHIPS.` · `LIKE A BEE, LIKE AN ANTHILL.` · `ONE TO LIVE, TWO TO WORK, ONE TO KEEP.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S DISCIPLINE.` · then, large: `FOUR PARTS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Without opening any app, picture your money in four piles, roughly as it is right now. How big is the part you live on? The part that builds something: your work, your skills, your future? The part kept for hard times? Don't calculate. Just notice the shape, and how it feels in the body to look at it. Then rest, and let one small adjustment suggest itself, if one does. The bell holds the time.
Four parts. The Buddha's advice to Sigala: one part to live on, two for work, and one kept for hard times.
Your line: four parts. Today, look at one line of your budget and ask which of the four parts it belongs to. Day three hundred eighty.

381.title: Work as practice
381.hook: a Chan saying tied to Baizhang: a day without work, a day without food
381.howItsDone: In Chan and Zen monasteries, daily work periods are part of the schedule, and residents and retreatants clean, cook and garden in silence as practice; in Japanese temples this is called samu.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four parts, and your line was the same. Which of the four parts did that budget line turn out to belong to? Day three hundred eighty-one.

An old Chan master, well past the age for field work, still goes out each day to work in the monastery fields with the younger monks. They worry about him. So one day they hide his tools. He doesn't argue. He just doesn't eat that day. When they ask him why, he answers, so the story goes: a day without work is a day without food. The master is Baizhang, of Tang-dynasty China, and the line has carried his name ever since. Today: work as practice.
screen: `AN OLD MAN IN THE FIELDS.` → `THE TOOLS GO MISSING.` → `A DAY WITHOUT WORK.`

segments.voice: Baizhang's name is tied to something new in Buddhist history. In India, by the old monastic rules, monks didn't farm or dig the soil. They walked for alms and lived on what the village gave. When the teaching traveled to China, things changed. Some monasteries stood in remote mountains, far from any village to feed them. Chan communities began to farm, cook, haul water and chop wood for themselves. Tradition credits Baizhang with the first rules for Chan monasteries, built around shared labor. The original text of those rules is lost, and some historians think much of the story was told later, but the ideal stuck. Work wasn't a break from practice. It was practice. In Japan the same idea carries the name samu: work done as meditation, sweeping, weeding, scrubbing, in silence and fully. That connects to right livelihood in a quiet way. Few jobs let you choose every task. You can choose how you're present for it. Sweeping a floor with your whole attention and sweeping it while rehearsing an argument are two different afternoons, even if the floor ends up equally clean. The saying is sometimes taken as a hard rule: no work, no lunch. The story suggests something gentler. Baizhang isn't punishing anyone, not even himself. For him, working and eating simply belonged together, the way breathing in and breathing out do. Leaving one out didn't make sense.
screen: `IN INDIA, MONKS DIDN'T FARM.` · `CHAN MONASTERIES PICK UP HOES.` · `SAMU: WORK AS MEDITATION.` · `TWO AFTERNOONS, ONE CLEAN FLOOR.` · then, large: `WORK IS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Choose one task you'll do today anyway: the dishes, an email, folding laundry, a spreadsheet. Picture doing it the Chan way. Not faster, not slower. Fully. Your hands on what they're touching. Your attention on this plate, this sentence, this towel. When the mind runs ahead to the next task, notice it, and come back to this one. Rehearse it here for a while, with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Work as practice. Baizhang's saying, a day without work is a day without food: in Chan, ordinary labor is part of the path.
Your line: work is practice. Today, do one job fully, with nothing else in your head, and notice how it feels when it's done. Day three hundred eighty-one.

382.title: Enough
382.hook: contentment is the greatest wealth (Dhammapada 204); greed makes any amount too little
382.howItsDone: Buddhist texts praise contentment often; monastics practice it by living with a few requisites, and lay Buddhists often reflect on it when they recite or study the Dhammapada and the Mangala Sutta, which lists contentment among the highest blessings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: work as practice, and your line, work is practice. Did one job get done fully, with nothing else in your head? Day three hundred eighty-two.

There was once a king, the old stories say, who could make it rain money. He would clap his hands, and gold coins would fall from the sky until they were knee-deep. He ruled the whole earth. Then he wanted heaven, and got it: first the heaven of the four great kings, then the higher heaven where Sakka, king of the gods, gave him half his throne. And sitting on half a throne in paradise, King Mandhatu had one small thought: why only half? Today: enough.
screen: `A KING WHO MAKES IT RAIN GOLD.` → `HALF A THRONE IN HEAVEN.` → `WHY ONLY HALF?`

segments.voice: The moment he thought it, the story says, his power drained away. He fell back to earth, into his own garden, an old man, and died there. The tradition tells this story alongside a short verse of the Dhammapada. In Max Müller's translation: "There is no satisfying lusts, even by a shower of gold pieces." A shower of gold. That's Mandhatu's rain. The point isn't that he wanted something wicked. It's that wanting has no built-in stopping point. Whatever amount you have, greed can make it feel too little. A raise can feel like enough for a while. Then the new number becomes the floor. Another verse, which you may remember from the first year, gives the alternative in four words. Müller has it: "contentedness the best riches." The Pali is santuṭṭhi: contentment, being satisfied with what's here. Notice it's called riches, not poverty. Contentment isn't settling for less, and it isn't a ban on ever wanting anything. In this tradition it's a kind of wealth you can actually keep, because it doesn't depend on the number. That closes these six days on livelihood. Earn clean. Watch what your money does. Count blamelessness above it all. Divide it wisely. Work with your whole attention. And then, at some point, say the one word greed can't say: enough.
screen: `HE FALLS BACK TO EARTH.` · `NO SATISFYING IT, EVEN WITH GOLD.` · `THE NEW NUMBER BECOMES THE FLOOR.` · `CONTENTMENT IS RICHES.` · then, large: `ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Look around the room, or picture your home. Pick one thing, a coat, your phone, your bed, the food in your kitchen, and say to yourself quietly: this is enough. Notice whether anything inside you argues. If it does, let it talk, and stay with the thing anyway. Then try one more. Then, perhaps, the breath itself: this breath is enough. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Enough. Santuṭṭhi, contentment: the Dhammapada calls it the best riches, because greed can make any amount feel too little.
Your line: enough. Today, name one thing that is enough, and stop looking for its upgrade. Day three hundred eighty-two.

383.title: Right effort
383.hook: four efforts: to prevent, to abandon, to arouse, to maintain (AN 4.13)
383.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often present right effort through the four right strivings, and practitioners use them to decide what a moment of practice needs: restraint, letting go, cultivating, or sustaining.

segments.voice: Yesterday: enough, and your line was the same. Did you name one thing that was enough, and leave its upgrade alone? Day three hundred eighty-three.

Anyone who has kept a garden knows there are four jobs. Keep weed seeds from blowing in. Pull the weeds that have already come up. Plant what you want to grow. And water what's already growing, so it doesn't wilt. Skip any one of them and the garden suffers, no matter how hard you work at the other three. The Buddha gave the sixth factor of his path the same four-part shape: two jobs about the harmful, two about the good. Today: right effort.
screen: `KEEP THE SEEDS OUT.` → `PULL WHAT CAME UP.` → `PLANT, AND WATER.`

segments.voice: Sammā vāyāma. Vāyāma means effort, exertion, striving. In the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha lays out four right strivings. First, for unwholesome states that haven't arisen: work so they don't arise. Second, for unwholesome states that have arisen: work to let them go. Third, for wholesome states that haven't arisen: work to bring them about. Fourth, for wholesome states that have arisen: work to keep them, so they don't fade, and to help them grow to fullness. In the next sutta over they get short names: restraint, abandoning, developing, protecting. For each one, the text uses the same string of verbs: you generate desire, make an effort, rouse energy, apply your mind, and strive. Desire is in there on purpose. The wish to do good is part of the engine. Notice two things about the shape. First, it's balanced. Half of right effort isn't about fighting the harmful at all. It's about growing and keeping the good. People new to practice often pour everything into the first two and forget the gardener's last two jobs. Second, each one asks for a different kind of effort. Preventing is quiet, like latching a gate. Abandoning is active, like pulling a weed. Arousing takes initiative, like planting. Maintaining takes patience, like daily watering. So the question isn't only am I trying hard enough. It's which of the four does this moment need. The next four days take them one at a time.
screen: `VĀYĀMA: EFFORT, STRIVING.` · `PREVENT, ABANDON, AROUSE, MAINTAIN.` · `HALF OF IT IS ABOUT THE GOOD.` · `WHICH ONE DOES THIS MOMENT NEED?` · then, large: `FOUR EFFORTS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Let your mind walk the last day like a gardener walking the rows. Is there something unhelpful you can see coming, a habit, a mood? That's for preventing. Something already sprouting that needs pulling? Something good you'd like to plant? Something good already growing that needs water? Don't fix anything. Just choose one of the four, and let your attention rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sammā vāyāma. Right effort: prevent, abandon, arouse, maintain. The sixth factor of the path.
Your line: four efforts. Today, make one of the four on purpose, and notice what kind of effort it asked of you. Day three hundred eighty-three.

384.title: Preventing
384.hook: guarding the sense doors so unhelpful states don't arise
384.howItsDone: Monastics practice sense restraint by keeping their gaze lowered on the alms round and avoiding entertainment; lay Buddhists often apply it on observance days and, today, to how they use screens and media.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma vayama, right effort, and your line, four efforts. Which of the four did you make on purpose, and what did it ask of you? Day three hundred eighty-four.

Someone opens their phone to check the weather. Forty minutes later they're watching a stranger renovate a bathroom in another country, vaguely annoyed, and a little less fond of their own bathroom. Nobody decided any of that. It came in through the eyes, one tap at a time. Nobody broke down the door. It was simply left open. Today, the first of the four efforts, the one that works before anything goes wrong: preventing.
screen: `JUST CHECKING THE WEATHER.` → `FORTY MINUTES LATER.` → `THE DOOR WAS LEFT OPEN.`

segments.voice: The Pali word for this effort is saṃvara, restraint, and the suttas give it a specific picture: guarding the doors of the senses. Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind: six doors. The standard passage goes like this. When a practitioner sees a form with the eye, they don't grab at its signs and features, the details that set wanting or irritation going. Because if the eye door were left unguarded, greedy and painful states could pour in. So they guard the eye. The same for the ear, and every other door. Notice what this doesn't say. It doesn't say shut your eyes, or never look at anything lovely. Seeing is fine. The guarding happens one step later, at the grabbing: the moment the mind zooms in, replays, wants more, or wants it gone. That's where the gatekeeper stands. The Dhammapada says it in one line, in Max Müller's words: "Restraint in the eye is good, good is restraint in the ear". The verse runs on through every door. It's a quiet effort, and easy to overlook. Abandoning a mood once it's raging is hard work. Not letting it in costs very little. It's the difference between fixing a slow leak and bailing out a flooded basement. And it's practical in a way the early monks could hardly have imagined. The doors now include a glowing rectangle, often built to keep the eyes on it.
screen: `SAṂVARA: RESTRAINT.` · `SIX DOORS OF THE SENSES.` · `GUARD AT THE GRAB, NOT THE GLANCE.` · `A SLOW LEAK, NOT A FLOOD.` · then, large: `GUARD THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, eyes open, gaze resting low. Let things come into view without following them. A color. A shape. A sound from outside. Each time the mind starts to grab, to zoom in, judge, or spin a story, notice it, and let the thing simply be seen, or simply be heard. You're standing at the gate, watching what comes through. Nothing has to be shut out. Nothing has to be chased. The bell holds the time.
Preventing. Saṃvara, restraint: guarding the sense doors so unhelpful states don't get in. The first of the four efforts.
Your line: guard the gate. Today, guard one door, your phone, a news feed, a certain kind of conversation, and notice what doesn't get in. Day three hundred eighty-four.

385.title: Abandoning
385.hook: five ways with a bad thought: replace it, see its danger, ignore it, calm its cause, and at last suppress it (MN 20)
385.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist schools teach these five methods for working with persistent thoughts, often recommending the gentler ones first and keeping forceful suppression for emergencies.

segments.voice: Yesterday: preventing, and your line, guard the gate. Which door did you guard, and what didn't get in? Day three hundred eighty-five, the end of the week.

Some thoughts get past the gate anyway. You're lying in bed and the argument from lunch starts replaying. Or a craving that won't quit. Or a worry, looping like a song you can't stand. Just let it go is easy advice to give. It rarely comes with instructions. The Buddha gave some. In one sutta he gives five ways, in order, from gentlest to strongest, each with its own picture. The first one is a carpenter's trick. Today: abandoning.
screen: `THE ARGUMENT REPLAYS.` → `JUST LET IT GO.` → `BUT HOW?`

segments.voice: The sutta is in the Middle Length Discourses, and its name means the stilling of thoughts. Way one: when an unwholesome thought keeps coming, turn the mind to another sign, one connected with the wholesome. If it's anger, kindness. If it's craving, something that cools it. Like a skilled carpenter, the Buddha says, who knocks out a coarse peg with a finer one. You don't yank the bad peg out; you drive a better one in, and it pushes the old one through. Way two: if that doesn't work, look at the danger in the thought. Where is this taking me? He compares it to a young person dressed up and fond of finery who'd be horrified to find a carcass hung around their neck. Way three: if it still comes, simply don't attend to it, like someone who closes their eyes or looks away from what they don't want to see. Way four: calm the thought's momentum. Like a man walking fast who asks, why am I hurrying? He slows down, then stands, then sits, then lies down. Way five, the last resort: teeth clenched, tongue pressed to the roof of the mouth, hold the mind down with the mind, like a strong man pinning a weaker one. The order is the lesson. Force comes last, not first. It's tempting to start at way five, and that's the one that wears a person out. Look back at the week. Blameless is best. Four parts. Work is practice. Enough. Four efforts. Guard the gate. And today: a finer peg.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Let a thought that's been bothering you come up: nothing overwhelming, something small and sticky. Notice what kind it is: irritation, craving, worry. Now choose its finer peg. For irritation, picture that person on a good day, laughing. For craving, the breath, cool and complete. For worry, one thing that's fine right now. Gently drive the new peg in, and let it push the old one through. The bell holds the time.
Abandoning. The second effort: letting go of unwholesome thoughts already here. The sutta gives five ways, gentlest first.
Your line: a finer peg. Today, when a sticky thought comes back, try the first way: drive in something wholesome in its place. Day three hundred eighty-five, and a week done.
